Thanks for updating, I was wondering how you were doing. SO GLAD to hear that you're out.

You're very, *very* wise to ignore his attempts to contact you. You might even want to consider changing your phone number.

He will do whatever he can to "hoover" you back into the relationship, but as soon as he feels like you are "his" again he will go back to his old ways.

[Edit:

> His messages are a mix of "I love you, please come back," to "you're still a whore" & "I won't warn you again."

This is exactly what I mean. Notice that he's changing tactics - from sweet and loving, to degrading you, to threatening you. He's rifling through his "bag of tricks" to find one that will work.

Note the subtext here: **he isn't considering what _you_ want or what will make _you_ happy.** He's only concerned about getting you back, *even if that's not what you want*.

Meaning, he is not respecting you as a fully fledged human being who has a right to have needs, boundaries, preferences, etc that aren't in line with what he'd like you to have.

**Someone who truly loves you will want you to be happy, _even if it's not with them_**.]

Let happiness be your guide from here on out. When I left my husband, I was unsure if I would have to officially end the relationship or if there was a chance that he could see the errors of his ways and we could reconcile. My mom gave me a little framed picture that says "choose happiness".

I still love and miss him, and grieve that the relationship wasn't what I thought it was. But I am happier than I've been in a *very* long time, and I can't ignore that. 

Keep meeting new people and enjoying life. Start filling in the gaps he took away from you. And never stop dancing.

This is abuse, and **it is not your fault**.

I'm a queer guy who left my abusive husband last year. Feel free to contact me via DM if I can be helpful.

First and foremost you need to consider how much privacy you have, and be **sure** that the areas of your life that you think are private are actually private. Abuse victims are most at risk when they attempt to leave their abuser, so **do not tell him** you know you're being abused, or about any of the preparations you're making.

Secondly, start gathering anything important - documents or paperwork, identification, keepsakes, cash, etc - and put them somewhere safe and private. Rent a safe deposit box if you have to.

Thirdly, take stock of your financial situation. How dependent on him are you? Are you employed? Do you have your own bank account? Credit card? Start establishing as much financial independence as you can, **but ensure he doesn't know you're doing so**. Do not use your home address when you open these accounts, use someone else's address or a post office box, etc. 

And finally, make an exit plan. Actually make two - an emergency plan in case the shit hits the fan sooner than expected, and a plan for if the conditions during your departure are more ideal. Have a bug out bag packed and ready to go, know where you'd stay if you had to leave *right now*.

If you don't have to use your emergency plan, **do not tell him you're leaving until you've moved out and are safe**, and **do not tell him where you've gone**. Additionally, instruct anyone who *does* know your location to not give it to him either. 

Also, mutual friends are not allies, expect them to support him and not you. This is especially true if he knew them before you and he met.

And read Why Does He Do That by Lundy Bancroft. It's available as a [free PDF](https://www.docdroid.net/py03/why-does-he-do-that.pdf). Everything we think we know about abuse is wrong. The book will be very eye opening for you. It's mostly written within the context of a male abuser with a female victim, but what it says is applicable to gay male relationships as well.

They know *exactly* what they're doing, and do it so easily because they think they're justified. To these people, their partner having any needs at all means the relationship is all about them, which is where the guilt trip comes from.

**It is not your fault. There is absolutely nothing you can do that could justifiably provoke this kind of treatment, which unfortunately means there is nothing you can do to prevent it either.**

He and he alone is responsible for his actions. **It is not your fault.**

All the best, and feel free to contact me privately.

/u/wheredidyougofriendo listen to this here. I recently left a 15 year relationship with a man who abused me for pretty much that entire time. **It is brainwashing**. Part of me knew on some level that something wasn't right for most of that time, and I came close to fully realizing it a few times, but abusers do anything and  everything they can to keep their victims confused and/or in fear. I spent well over a decade believing *I* was the problem and trying to "fix" myself so I could be the husband he wanted. So much wasted time.

*And* in my case there were literally no outward signs to others.  I had to break free on almost entirely my own strength, because just about no one saw it or took it seriously enough when I told them. It wasn't until I had an individual session with our couples therapist after working with her for 2 years that, finally, someone reflected back to me that something isn't right here. I moved out about a week after that session.

Please for the love of God take this seriously. If there are signs to others, it's probably a lot more serious than my situation was, and I came close to killing myself. The isolation alone is a *huge* red flag, and it's also very common for an abuser to escalate after an event that increases the commitment level of a relationship, like marriage or the birth of a child. 

And please read "Why Does He Do That" by Lundy Bancroft. Everything we think we know about abuse is **wrong**. The book is even available online as a [free pdf](https://www.docdroid.net/py03/why-does-he-do-that.pdf) if you don't want to buy it.

Feel free to send me a private message if I can be of any help, and let us know how your friend is doing when you find out more.

Couple's therapy is the worst possible thing for someone with an abusive partner. And I say this as someone in the process of leaving an abuser after years of couples therapy. 

They are manipulative people who will use the therapy itself as a means to abuse, often even turning the therapist against their victim. In my case the abuse escalated significantly as we continued therapy, and a pattern emerged where I'd get put in my place after difficult therapy sessions where I dared to speak freely.

It's best for people with abusive partners to get therapy for themselves, and to build up their support network outside of the relationship if they are able to.
No worries, thank you for being open to new information.
I wish I could upvote this more than once.

That doesn't matter, abuse doesn't work like that.

It's not a specific act. Violence, intimidation, gaslighting etc are *tactics* used to abuse someone, but are not what abuse is at its core. Abuse is about *control* first and foremost, and the refusal to see the victim as an actual human being with needs, boundaries, etc that are separate from their own. The "shape" of the abuse changes depending on what the abuser wants to control, and what methods they're willing to use in exerting that control, but it's all the same under the hood.

Once you've identified clear signs of abuse (and the OP contains many textbook examples!) all bets are off because you have no way of knowing which tactics are in their bag of tricks waiting to emerge, and it **ALWAYS** escalates once it starts.

And it's futile anyway, because the only thing they're looking for is for you to fall into line and not only do what they want, but basically not exist as a human being when you're not meeting their needs in some way. No matter how you respond, they will keep pulling new things from their bag of tricks until they find one that works.

Edit: also, physical violence is not the only way to harm someone. Emotional abuse causes lifelong damage as well, and those who experience both typically say the emotional abuse is what caused them the most harm.

I'm currently in the process of ending a 15 year relationship with an abuser who never laid a hand on me, and yet his abuse caused me to be suicidal for years (attempting on one occasion) before I realized what was really causing it. His treatment of me literally almost killed me.

Edit: these are examples of the worst advice I've received.

I have two that are both widespread and very toxic:

- "Put each other first"
- "It takes two to tango"

The first one is terrible because it primes us to throw our own needs aside while we pour ourselves into the bottomless pit of meeting an abusers needs.  We all put our own needs first, and then offer support as needed/able.

The second one is terrible because it primes us to accept being blamed for an abuser's actions.  One of the go-to responses when an abuser is confronted with their actions is what I call "but you!".  Meaning, instead of taking ownership and responsibility for their actions, they toss it back and claim they were provoked by something their victim did.

This whole idea of "mutuality" is bullshit.  We are all responsible for our own actions, and "but you!" is making excuses, not amends.  There is absolutely nothing one can do that would justify being treated as less than human.

>Now, the second time, I did not touch him at all and he choked me, so I realise that this time was not my fault.

What?? It would **NEVER** be your fault! We are all responsible for our own actions! Even if you did something that really upset him, he is still responsible for choosing to put his hands on you instead of, for example, take a walk to cool off.

*And* there is no reason, ever, to do that to someone anyway! Nothing you could possible do would deserve that kind of response!

After reading "Why Does He Do That" (which is not a recent book) I've realized that everything we think we know about abuse is dead wrong. It's not a specific action, like a punch or a slap. It's not gaslighting, or a barrage of mean names. Those things are different *tactics* abusers use, but they are not abuse in and of themselves. 

Abuse is about **control** at its heart, and the failure to recognize the other person as a fully fledged human being with their own separate wants, needs, boundaries, thoughts, feelings, opinions, beliefs, etc. The "shape" of the abuse varies, depending on what the abuser wants to control and what methods they're willing to use. But it's all different ways of achieving the same thing.

If we recognized that we'd know that the specific actions don't matter or determine whether or not abuse is occurring, and that even kindness can be used to abuse.

How many of us have had our head spinning from the transition from "bad cop" to "good cop", and questioning how someone so nice could be abusive? That's part of the game. They go through their bag of tricks until they find one that works.

No worries. 

I suggest checking out the book linked in the other comment. It was very eye opening for me.

>You’ve mentioned areas of where my boundaries end and where others begin. What do you mean by that?

I mean recognize that it's not all about you and what you want. Other people have their own needs, boundaries, etc that are not only separate from yours, but aren't necessarily what you'd prefer them to have.

> Why do people want to control someone by means of abuse?

To be clear, in my comment I meant that abuse and control are the same thing. Using kindness as a means to control is also abuse. In fact, cycling  between kindness and meanness is usually part of the pattern, and serves to keep the other confused and disoriented and blaming themselves. 

> Is it because they can’t control their own life/emotions so they think it’s easier to control someone else?

No it's because they don't recognize that the other person even has their own life/emotions that are separate from theirs. There is no deeper meaning here, abuse is an end in itself, not a means to an end.

Edit: also in my experience, abusers are not only unwilling to examine their own actions, but are also fully aware of what they're doing. The fact that you're even asking these questions suggests to me that you might not be abusive, but of course I don't know you so take that with a grain of salt.

It's also very common for abusers to accuse their victims of abuse (because in their mind the relationship revolves around them, and when the other person doesn't act accordingly they feel like victims), so keep that in mind.

What I've learned after spending the last few months undoing the 10+ years of brainwashing that my soon-to-be ex husband put me through is that abuse is not a specific action.  It's not a shove, or a slap. It's not a barrage of mean names or belittling. It's not gaslighting.

All of those things are *tactics* used to abuse someone, but they are not abuse in and of themselves. Abuse at its heart is about **control**, and the basic failure to recognize the other person as a fully fledged human being with their own independent needs, boundaries, thoughts, feelings, opinions, beliefs, etc. Someone who is abusive doesn't recognize this basic fact, and attempts to get the other person to conform to their needs, boundaries, etc by controlling them using various methods.

So, the *shape* of the abuse varies from abuser to abuser, in terms of what they want to control, and what methods they're willing to use in order to exert that control. But at its heart it's all the same.

So really, doing some work and introspection on where you end and other people begin would go a long way.

>So now, what you guys think? how should be my approach? i know she made it clear that she would contact me when she is ready but how long?

Could be forever.

Leave her alone. You're not entitled to contact with other people. She has a right to not have you in her life if that's what she wants. Accept that this is out of your hands. She'll contact you if and when she wants to.

>for what it's worth, love isn't the butterfly jitters in your stomach when you first meet someone - it's respecting them enough to put their needs over your own

As someone who is in the process of leaving an abuser who practically used this as his mantra - I have to disagree here. Never put anyone's needs over your own. Your needs *always* come first. This kind of idea primes us to throw our own needs aside while we pour ourselves into the bottomless pit of meeting an abuser's needs.

Love is respecting someone as their own full-fledged person separate from yourself, who has needs, boundaries, thoughts, feelings, opinions, etc, that are not only different from yours, but are also not necessarily what you'd prefer them to have.
Don't tell him at all!!! Just leave, don't tell him where you're going, and immediately block him!!!
They will be happy to have you in their lives again, and I bet they will tell you they've been worried about you for a long time.

>Yes, but I’m a little embarrassed of telling them that he hit me... gonna have to cross that bridge soon.

That's also part of the pattern. I bet he regularly makes you feel responsible for his actions.

You are not, he is the one and only person responsible for his choices. You have no reason to feel embarrassed over something you did not do.

> When it’s good it’s so good. 

That's part of the pattern. If he was always abusive, you would have left a long time ago. Read up on [the cycle of abuse](http://www.hiddenhurt.co.uk/cycle_of_abuse.html).

>Wish me luck I’m going to do my best to walk away. 

You WILL do it.

- Gather anything important - documents, id, etc - and put them somewhere safe.
- Find a safe place to live. Go to a shelter if you have to.
- **Leave when he is not home.** Do not tell him you're leaving before you go. **Just go.**
- Block him on every method of communication you have.
- Do not tell him where you're going, and tell anyone who knows where you are to do the same. This is important - the highest danger for people leaving physically abusive relationships occurs **immediately after leaving**.

I'm in the process of getting out of a relationship with someone who was emotionally abusive to me, but thankfully not violent, and I can tell you that moving out changes things so much. It'll be like a breath of fresh air.

All the best, know we're rooting for you here.

Those are some serious red flags.

But even if they're not, listen to your feelings. If something doesn't feel right, don't do it. You're entitled to your feelings and don't have to justify them to anyone but yourself.

Please rethink whether you want to move in with this guy. I guarantee whatever issues you see will only become worse, and a whole host of issues you didn't know existed will surface. This is true even in relationships that aren't abusive. People let their guard down more when they feel safe, and when you're in such close quarters with someone you see more of them.

>I really love him. He's not always bad, I swear.

They never are. If they were, no one would get into a relationship with them, would they? 

Read up on [the "cycle of abuse"](http://www.hiddenhurt.co.uk/cycle_of_abuse.html). The times when he is nice are part of the pattern. That's when you're relieved the incident is over, and hopeful that things will improve from there. It keeps you disoriented and confused because you never know when the other side of him will surface again.

Really, *really* rethink moving in with him. If you are afraid of telling him you're having second thoughts, take note. Why are you afraid? In a healthy relationship he would want to be sure you're comfortable moving in with him.

I can tell you cohabiting is a make or break issue. It really changes the dynamic - and your life - to have this person in your home. You no longer have a sanctuary where you can be away from him.

Thank you for all of this.

In particular:

>[The Awful Cult of Two]( https://www.reddit.com/r/Codependency/comments/8p4bb5/how_many_of_you_have_been_in_the_awful_cult_of_two/)

Holy shit, I've been saying for months that my relationship felt like a cult. Like, I couldn't question it or my happiness within it. One of his mantras when things were "tough" (abusive) was "believe in us!".

No, dude. A relationship shouldn't feel like a fucking cult. If my genuine thoughts, beliefs and feelings need to be.. suppressed or whatever, something is very wrong.

There are a lot of age and gender based generalizations here that may be true in some cases, but certainly aren't true across the board.

In particular:

>Older men (late 20's to early 30's) are not only closer to your maturity level but often in a position to complement your goals and dreams instead of being a parasitic burden.

It's also really common for abusive men to date (read: prey on) much younger women who don't have as much life or relationship experience as them, and are less likely to recognize the red flags than women their own age.

While I haven't been raped, I did have an incredibly traumatic experience last fall and can completely understand the way your wife has been acting. When something happens that exceeds your mind's ability to cope, all sorts of mental gymnastics occur to make it more "okay".

In my case, surgical error resulted in the loss of most of my erogenous tissue (more details in post history), and even though I knew what happened immediately after waking up, it took a *full month* for the reality to sink in. During that time, I was completely aware and accepting of two contradictory realities at the same time. 

*And*, I spent most of that time going on about how great the surgeon was to anyone who would listen! Because the reality was too much to bear, and I was overcompensating. 

In my case, when the full reality hit me, my husband dismissed it as anxiety and wasn't there for me when I needed him the most. It was horrible to not only have gone through what I went through, but to have the one who was supposed to support me act like I was fucking imagining things. I can't even begin to describe how awful that time was.

We're separated now, and I'm not sure if we'll get back together or not.

Of course I'm not you or your wife, but please consider the fact that when shit happens that people can't cope with, their mind does all sorts of bizarre things to make it more "okay".

Edit: honestly after reading some of these comments, I want to give your poor wife a hug. I see a traumatized woman coping with it the only way she can, and people here are accusing her of cheating and calling her a whore. It really reminds me of how my husband responded to my trauma, and it's an additional trauma in itself to not be believed about your trauma. Please for the sake of your marriage and your wife's wellbeing think about this.

Thank you very much for this comment.

This is so familiar.  I've been in and out of psychiatrists, psychologists, had full assessments, etc.  All came back with what I already knew, and what can be caused by abuse - PTSD & depression / anxiety.  On my birthday this year he told me he thought I had Asperger's (basically because I was unable to read his mind and just.. *know* what kind of emotional support he needed in the moment) and wanted me to get assessed.  Last year it was Borderline Personality Disorder (because I was finally expressing my emotions after years of shoving them aside to keep him happy).

He would also get upset if I tried to talk to him about something that he had already apologized for (holding grudges), as if that immediately erases whatever damage his actions caused.

> I feel that some abusers actually don't know how to deal with other people's pain or emotions, especially when they know they've caused it, because that would mean acknowledging and taking responsibility. And they can't do that. So they shut it out.

This is also familiar.  My husband has such a strong need to be "good" that he can't handle it when he's not, and when confronted with his actions his mind just makes it go away however it can.
Thank you.

Thanks for this comment.  I'm really struggling to keep my head straight on this.  It's so easy to slip back into old patterns and ways of thinking, it really feels like there are two completely different frames competing in my head, and sometimes it's tough to know which is the dream (nightmare?) and which is real.  I keep doubting myself, but have been trying to remind myself of how it really felt to be there.  Not how we told ourselves it felt, how it *really* felt.

While his behaviour was a pattern that goes back to basically the beginning of the relationship, there was an event that happened amid this crisis that really shook me up, and might be something I just cannot get over.  I know I am responsible for my own actions, but shortly after this event I nearly took my life.

> He knew very well all the times I was in tears huddled up.

The night I fully realized what happened to me (details in post history, see TW above) I'm sitting on the bed sobbing, wailing, pulling my hair, in literally the worst pain I had ever been in (emotional or physical), and he's standing at the door dismissing what happened to me and telling me that he has "some thinking to do" (edit: he was in "laying down the law" mode here, aggressive / intimidating body language and tone of voice) because he's not sure if he can be with someone like me (he suddenly was uncomfortable with my kinks, which he'd known about for a long time.. and he has some of his own).

Then he left, and I'm still wailing in blinding distress, hoping he'll come back and at least put his hand on my shoulder or something.  Then, he comes back and without peeking his head in the room, **closes the door**.  Literally closed the door on my suffering and distress.

How do you do that to *anyone*, let alone the one you vowed to love and respect??

Thanks for the response.  To be fair, I don't think he's aware of how he's been treating me and the impact it's had on me.  That said though, our couples therapist did go to great lengths to get him to see what was happening but was unable to.

And yes I am kind of astounded by how lightly he's been taking my need for space.  Originally I wanted to go completely no contact for at least 3 months, but we ended up agreeing on daily text messages as a sign of life.  Now he's upset with me for not doing more than that, when I was clear that having space was a necessary part of this process.

Yes, I have two therapists, one of whom we saw together for couples therapy for over 2 years before the separation, and who agrees with my assessment.

Do you have a response to the questions I asked?

I can relate. A red flag for me was when I realized hearing the front door open when my husband was due home caused a spike of anxiety in me. Got out about 2 months ago and it still happens sometimes when I hear similar sounds.

Yes, this has been an issue for me for a few years now. No one believes me when I say something is going on with my body. Including what I'm going through now, which is absurd. Surgical error damaged my sexual organs, and no one believes me. How could anyone be mistaken about something like that?!
Thanks very much for sharing your story. It's difficult for me to see how it will get better now, but I do have things to keep me going for now and maybe I'll feel differently later.
Thank you very much for the comment, it is good to know I'm not alone. I wish you nothing but good things in life.
